First, one factual correction I’d make before you explain it to your partner: **Proton is not an American startup out of San Francisco.** Proton (Proton AG) is a **Swiss** company, and that’s a meaningful part of its privacy positioning. If you say “American startup” to your partner, it’s both inaccurate and weaker than the actual “Swiss-based” point.

## Fresh practical comparison

### 1. Cost

**Gmail**
- Free tier gives you **15GB**, but that storage is shared with Gmail, Drive, and Photos.
- If you need more, you’d pay for Google One, but for basic email use, $0/month.

**Proton Mail**
- Free tier is only **1GB**.
- The paid **15GB Mail+ plan is about $4/month** or roughly **$48/year**.

**Practical takeaway:**  
Proton is **not** the cheaper storage deal. If the argument is purely “how much storage per dollar,” Gmail wins, especially if your partner is the cost-conscious one. The honest practical framing for Proton is:

> “We pay $4/month not for more storage, but for private email without ad/personalization-based scanning, under Swiss law.”

If you need **100GB+** for Drive/Photos/files, Gmail + Google One is likely more practical and often cheaper per GB. But if the issue is **personal email privacy**, then $4/month is a small recurring cost.

---

### 2. Convenience

**Gmail**
- Excellent mobile app.
- Excellent desktop web interface.
- Works well with Google Calendar, Drive, Docs, Meet, Contacts, etc.
- Very good search.
- Easy to use with third-party clients.
- If you already live in the Google ecosystem, Gmail is the low-friction choice.

**Proton Mail**
- Clean web and mobile apps.
- Free tier is mostly confined to Proton’s own apps/web interface.
- Paid plans add more flexibility, including standard IMAP/SMTP-style access in some setups, but it’s still less smooth than Gmail and you lose some Proton-specific encryption conveniences if using a third-party client.
- Less deep integration with the rest of your life unless you also adopt Proton Calendar/Drive, which may not replace Google for you.

**Practical takeaway:**  
On day-to-day convenience, **Gmail is stronger**, especially for someone already using Google Calendar/Drive. Proton is “good enough,” but it is not more convenient than Gmail.

If you try to make the case to your partner on convenience alone, Gmail wins. The Proton case works better if you say:

> “I don’t need Gmail-level convenience from my personal email. I mainly need it to be private, easy to check, and stable.”

---

### 3. Search

**Gmail**
- One of the best email search experiences available.
- You can search phrases, attachments, dates, sender/recipient, etc.
- Very useful if your email is a long-term archive.

**Proton Mail**
- Search is more limited because the company cannot index encrypted content the same way.
- You can still find messages, but it’s not as good for “find that one thing from three years ago.”

**Practical takeaway:**  
If your email is basically a personal inbox you check daily, Proton’s search may be fine.  
If your email is a searchable archive of receipts, travel confirmations, old messages, and attachments, Gmail is much more useful.

A realistic Proton argument would be:

> “My email isn’t a giant searchable archive. It’s correspondence, not a documentation system.”

That’s only true if it’s actually true for your usage.

---

### 4. Spam and filtering

**Gmail**
- Very mature spam filter.
- Trained on massive volumes of email.
- Generally better at catching spam, phishing, and unwanted mail.

**Proton Mail**
- Has spam filtering.
- Probably “good enough” for many people.
- But it doesn’t have the same scale and maturity as Gmail.

**Practical takeaway:**  
If you get a lot of newsletters, promos, banking alerts, and random spam, Gmail will probably keep your inbox cleaner. Proton is acceptable, but Gmail is more polished in this area.

---

### 5. Storage and attachments

**Gmail**
- 15GB shared across Gmail, Drive, Photos.
- Great if you use Gmail/Drive/Photos as one ecosystem.
- Can be a downside if your Drive/Photos usage eats up your 15GB.

**Proton Mail**
- 15GB is for mail, not broadly shared with the same cloud-drive ecosystem unless you pay for separate Proton services.
- If you only use it for email and attachments, 15GB is plenty for most people.
- If you import years of old Gmail data, 1GB free is almost certainly too small.

**Practical takeaway:**  
For a new email account with modest attachment use, Proton’s paid 15GB can be enough. But if your email includes lots of files, photos, PDFs, or you plan to migrate years of historical Gmail data, storage becomes a real thing to measure.

---

### 6. Ecosystem lock-in

**Gmail**
- Deep Google integration is a big practical advantage, but also a big practical cost if you want privacy.
- If you use Android, Google Photos, Drive, Maps, Calendar, Docs, Meet, etc., Gmail fits naturally.

**Proton Mail**
- Standalone.
- You can use Proton as personal email while still using Google for everything else, but then your privacy gain is narrower: mainly your email content, not your whole digital life.

**Practical takeaway:**  
If you are already heavily in Google’s orbit, switching email to Proton helps, but it is not a total privacy reset. You may still have a Google account for Calendar/Photos/Drive. That’s fine, but it changes the framing.

A practical way to explain it:

> “I’m not giving up Google. I’m separating my personal email from Google’s ecosystem so that my personal correspondence isn’t scanned for ads/personalization.”

That’s a clean, practical boundary.

---

### 7. Migration and switching cost

This is a real practical cost, and it is not trivial.

Moving to Proton means:
- Creating the new address.
- Updating accounts.
- Updating payment profiles.
- Updating two-factor authentication recovery methods.
- Forwarding or importing old mail, if desired.
- Dealing with services that send confirmation emails to the old address.
- Possibly keeping Gmail around for Google-specific services.

Gmail, by contrast, means zero switching cost if you stay.

**Practical takeaway:**  
You should not pretend the migration is free. A fair argument to your partner would be:

> “There is a one-time administrative cost to switching, but it’s much smaller than a recurring privacy trade-off. I don’t want to pay with my personal correspondence every month just to keep things convenient.”

That’s a defensible practical framing: you’re paying a one-time inconvenience to avoid an ongoing exposure.

---

## If I weighed them purely on practical merits, without assuming your preference

Gmail is the more practical choice if you prioritize:
- Low cost.
- Excellent search.
- Deep integration with Google Calendar/Drive/Photos.
- Polished mobile/web experience.
- Strong spam filtering.
- Low migration hassle.
- Using email as a productivity/archive tool.

Proton Mail becomes more practical if you prioritize:
- No ad/personalization-based scanning of your personal mail.
